sections.title: Gram-positive cover: penicillins, glycopeptides and MRSA agents

blocks.text: **Beta-lactams are bactericidal.** They competitively block the transpeptidases (**penicillin-binding proteins, PBPs**) that cross-link peptidoglycan. **Glycopeptides** (vancomycin, teicoplanin) also stop cell-wall building, but they do it by clinging to the **D-alanine ends of peptidoglycan precursors**. Both groups kill in a **time-dependent** way: what matters is how long the level stays above the MIC. That is why benzylpenicillin is given 4-hourly in severe infection.

blocks.title: Penicillin families at a glance
rows: Gram-positives and anaerobes. **Strep. pyogenes is still sensitive everywhere.** Most staphylococci make penicillinase, so they are resistant
**Mainstay for meticillin-sensitive Staph. aureus (MSSA)**. Useless against MRSA
Penicillin spectrum plus Enterobacteriaceae, but E. coli resistance is common (about 57% across Europe in 2014). **Not suitable as empirical Gram-negative cover**
Clavulanate or sulbactam restores activity against beta-lactamase producers
Strong Gram-negative cover, including Pseudomonas (see next section)

blocks.title: Gram-positive organisms: Davidson’s suggested agents
rows: Penicillin; clindamycin or vancomycin as alternatives
Ampicillin, or a glycopeptide as the alternative
Vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin, clindamycin, tetracyclines, tigecycline, co-trimoxazole; rifampicin only as part of a combination

blocks.title: How Gram-positives escape
items: **MRSA:** the _mecA_ gene codes for **PBP2a**, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams. Flucloxacillin and meticillin can no longer stop cross-linking.

**VRE:** the cell-wall precursor ends in **D-Ala-D-Lac** instead of D-Ala-D-Ala, so vancomycin and teicoplanin cannot bind. The only oral option is linezolid; IV options are daptomycin and tigecycline.
Some MRSA strains also show reduced glycopeptide susceptibility because their cell wall becomes relatively impermeable.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.title: Reserve agents for resistant Gram-positives
rows: Gram-positive only: MRSA, ampicillin-resistant enterococci. Not absorbed orally, so **oral vancomycin treats C. difficile**. Keep IV vancomycin pre-dose levels >10 mg/L (15–20 mg/L in serious staphylococcal infection)
“Red man” histamine reaction if infused too fast; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, especially alongside aminoglycosides
IV only; bactericidal against Gram-positives including MRSA and GRE (skin infection, Staph. aureus endocarditis). No Gram-negative activity
**Fails in community-acquired pneumonia**; raised creatine kinase; eosinophilic pneumonitis
Oral or IV for MRSA and GRE; excellent oral bioavailability
**MAO-inhibitor activity: serotonin syndrome with SSRIs**; long courses cause marrow suppression (mainly thrombocytopenia, so FBC weekly) and peripheral/optic neuropathy
Gram-positive cocci and anaerobes; concentrates in bone (osteomyelitis); damps down TSST-1 and alpha-toxin in severe streptococcal or staphylococcal cellulitis

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection
Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.text: **Macrolides** (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) and **lincosamides** are bacteriostatic and bind the **same ribosomal site**, so they are never combined. Macrolides are the classic choice for **Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Bordetella**. Side effects: GI upset (about 30% of young adults on erythromycin), cholestatic jaundice with erythromycin estolate, and **QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes**. Macrolides also interact with theophylline, carbamazepine, digoxin and ciclosporin, so the doses of those drugs sometimes need adjusting.

A ladder for remembering cover: **amoxicillin** (strep, Listeria, enterococci) → **co-amoxiclav** (adds staph, Haemophilus, E. coli) → **piperacillin–tazobactam** (adds Pseudomonas) → **meropenem** (adds ESBL producers). Add **vancomycin/teicoplanin for MRSA** and a macrolide or doxycycline for atypicals.
Three classic traps: **rifampicin must never be given alone** for MRSA (resistance appears fast); **daptomycin does not work for pneumonia**; and **linezolid with an SSRI** risks serotonin syndrome.

Serious hepatitis is a recognised beta-lactam effect, mainly with **flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav**. Kumar notes that co-amoxiclav and flucloxacillin cause cholestatic jaundice about six times as often as plain amoxicillin.

sections.title: Gram-negative cover: cephalosporins, carbapenems, aminoglycosides and others

blocks.title: Cephalosporin generations
rows: Keeps Gram-positive cover, wider Gram-negative; cephamycins also hit anaerobic Gram-negative bacilli
Better Gram-negative cover; **ceftazidime covers Pseudomonas**. Ceftriaxone is once daily, so suits OPAT
Broad: streptococci and Gram-negatives **including P. aeruginosa**
**Cover MRSA**, plus Gram-negatives; ceftobiprole also covers P. aeruginosa

blocks.title: Cephalosporin rules to remember
items: **No cephalosporin covers enterococci** (ceftobiprole is the one exception).
**ESBLs inactivate every cephalosporin.**
Use is strongly linked to **C. difficile** infection.
Third-generation agents reach the CSF, so ceftriaxone is used for empirical meningitis; 1st- and 2nd-generation drugs are not used for CNS infection.

blocks.title: Other beta-lactams for Gram-negatives
rows: Gram-positives, Gram-negatives (including P. aeruginosa) and anaerobes
Aerobic Gram-negatives only (not ESBL producers); no Gram-positive or anaerobic activity
IV only. **Safe in most penicillin-allergic patients**, except those allergic to **ceftazidime** (same side chain)
Widest beta-lactam spectrum: Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes, **but not MRSA**
**Ertapenem misses Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter.** Imipenem is paired with cilastatin. Imipenem and ertapenem can provoke seizures, so **meropenem is the carbapenem for meningitis**

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.title: Gram-negative organisms: Davidson’s suggested agents
rows: Amoxicillin, trimethoprim, cefuroxime, ciprofloxacin, co-amoxiclav (local resistance decides)
Meropenem, ertapenem, ciprofloxacin, temocillin, aminoglycosides (if sensitive)
Ciprofloxacin, piperacillin–tazobactam, aztreonam, meropenem, aminoglycosides, ceftazidime or cefepime
Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, macrolides, cefuroxime, cefotaxime, ciprofloxacin

blocks.text: **Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) work mainly against Gram-negatives and act synergistically with beta-lactams. Their killing is **concentration-dependent** (it rises with the Cmax : MIC ratio), so they are given **once, at a high dose (gentamicin 7 mg/kg)**. A level taken **6–14 hours after the dose** is read on the **Hartford nomogram** to set a 24-, 36- or 48-hourly interval. For synergy in endocarditis, gentamicin is given in small divided doses with targets of pre-dose <1 mg/L and post-dose 3–5 mg/L. Oral absorption and **CSF penetration are negligible**.

blocks.title: Aminoglycoside toxicity
items: **Nephrotoxicity**: usually reversible; worse with other nephrotoxins.
**Cochlear damage**: irreversible; the risk rises with age and with an inherited mitochondrial mutation.
**Neuromuscular blockade** after rapid IV infusion: potentiated by **myasthenia gravis**, calcium-channel blockers and low magnesium.
Monitor renal function and levels, and keep courses short.

blocks.note: Look at: the Hartford nomogram. The plasma gentamicin level (y-axis) at 6–14 h after a 7 mg/kg dose (x-axis) falls in a 24-, 36- or 48-hourly band.
Look at: the single-dose concentration curve with Cmax, MIC line, time above MIC and AUC. Concentration-dependent drugs depend on Cmax : MIC; time-dependent drugs depend on time above MIC.

blocks.title: Non-beta-lactam Gram-negative agents
rows: Block DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Ciprofloxacin covers Pseudomonas, but resistance develops quickly. Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin add pneumococcal cover; moxifloxacin also covers anaerobes and mycobacteria
Tendinitis and **Achilles rupture** (older people, steroids); delirium and seizures; **QT prolongation**; raise theophylline levels; ciprofloxacin use is linked to MRSA and C. difficile ribotype 027
Disrupts the Gram-negative outer membrane: P. aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, carbapenemase producers. A **last-resort** drug
Strict anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium spp.), amoebae and Giardia; good brain and CSF levels
Metallic taste; **disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol**; neuropathy with long use
Blocks two successive steps of folate synthesis. **First-line for Pneumocystis jirovecii**
Trimethoprim resembles amiloride: **hyperkalaemia** (especially with ACE inhibitors). Sulphonamides: Stevens–Johnson/TEN, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Borrelia, H. pylori. Tigecycline covers MRSA and ESBL producers but not Pseudomonas
Avoid in children and pregnancy (teeth and bone); phototoxicity; tigecycline showed excess mortality in trials
Not for pyelonephritis or anything outside the bladder; long courses can cause lung fibrosis and neuropathy

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.title: Antimicrobials in pregnancy (Davidson)
rows: Chloramphenicol (grey baby syndrome); fluconazole (high doses); quinolones; sulphonamides (neonatal haemolysis); tetracyclines; trimethoprim in the first trimester
Penicillins, cephalosporins, erythromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, glycopeptides, linezolid, meropenem, aciclovir

blocks.text: **ESBL producers:** for serious infection use a **carbapenem**, even if the lab reports piperacillin–tazobactam as sensitive. Piperacillin–tazobactam did worse than a carbapenem in a trial. Once-daily ertapenem allows OPAT.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.text: A good blood level of gentamicin is useless in **meningitis**, because almost none crosses into the CSF. Always ask whether the drug reaches the site of infection.

blocks.title: First-line antituberculous drugs
rows: Activated by mycobacterial KatG; inhibits InhA, blocking **mycolic acid** synthesis. Cleared by hepatic acetylation
Hepatitis; **peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine 10 mg daily)**; hypersensitivity
Inhibits DNA-dependent **RNA polymerase**; bactericidal, also sterilises necrotic foci
**Potent P450 inducer** (contraceptive pill, warfarin and many others fail); **orange urine, tears and secretions**; hepatitis; flu-like symptoms; rarely thrombocytopenia
Kills semidormant bacilli in an acidic environment
Hepatitis; **raised urate (gout)**; myalgia, nausea. **M. bovis is intrinsically resistant**
Inhibits arabinosyl transferase (cell wall arabinogalactan); bacteriostatic; renally excreted; poor CSF penetration
**Optic (retrobulbar) neuritis**: red–green colour loss, falling acuity, central scotoma

blocks.title: Standard regimens and durations
items: Fully sensitive pulmonary TB: **2 months HRZE, then 4 months HR = 6 months**.
Keep all four drugs beyond 2 months if susceptibility results are still pending.
**TB meningitis: 12 months**; bone TB: 9 months (KC Essentials).
Treatment failure is mostly due to prescribing errors and poor adherence; **directly observed therapy (DOT)** helps.
Never use one drug alone: **combination therapy prevents resistance** emerging.

blocks.title: Drug-resistant TB
items: **MDR-TB** = resistant to **isoniazid and rifampicin**.
**XDR-TB** = MDR plus resistance to **any fluoroquinolone and at least one injectable** second-line drug (amikacin, capreomycin or kanamycin).
Second-line drugs: moxifloxacin/levofloxacin, injectable aminoglycosides, cycloserine (neurological effects), ethionamide, linezolid (good CSF penetration).
Newer agents **bedaquiline and delamanid prolong the QT interval**, so take care when combining them with fluoroquinolones.

blocks.title: Other mycobacterial uses
items: Latent TB at risk of reactivation: isoniazid + rifampicin for 3 months, or isoniazid alone for 6 months.
Rifampicin (or ciprofloxacin) is prophylaxis for close contacts of meningococcal disease.
**M. bovis** (unpasteurised milk, farm and abattoir workers; often lymph nodes) is treated with **isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol**, because pyrazinamide resistance is the rule.
**M. avium-intracellulare** in advanced HIV (CD4 <50/mm³) resists standard therapy: use **ethambutol + rifabutin + clarithromycin**.
Active pulmonary TB in hospital: isolate (negative-pressure room) until established on treatment, usually about 2 weeks.

blocks.text: **Ethambutol:** check visual acuity (Snellen) and colour vision (Ishihara) **before starting**. Stopping the drug when symptoms appear usually lets vision recover.

**Drug-induced hepatitis:** isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are all hepatotoxic. A mild transaminase rise is common. **Stop the drugs only if bilirubin rises or transaminases exceed three times normal**, then reintroduce them one at a time.

blocks.title: Antiviral drugs: mechanism, use and toxicity
rows: Guanosine analogues; **viral thymidine kinase** phosphorylates them, then they block viral DNA polymerase, so only infected cells are hit
HSV (IV for encephalitis, 2–3 weeks), VZV (chickenpox, shingles)
Very little; **crystals in renal tubules** with high-dose IV, so hydrate well
Phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase
**First-line for CMV disease** in the immunosuppressed (reserved for life- or sight-threatening infection)
Renal impairment, **electrolyte disturbance**, genital ulcers, neurotoxicity
CMV (including most ganciclovir-resistant strains), resistant HSV
**Neuraminidase inhibitors**: stop release of new virions; influenza A and B
Treatment within 48 h, and prophylaxis in high-risk groups
Blocks the M2 ion channel (influenza A only)
Largely obsolete because resistance is widespread
Lassa fever (IV); RSV in infants (inhaled); combination therapy for hepatitis C

blocks.title: Influenza regimens (high-risk patients)
items: **Treatment:** oral oseltamivir 75 mg BD, or zanamivir 10 mg BD by inhaler, for **5 days**; start within 48 h of symptom onset.
**Post-exposure prophylaxis:** same drugs **once daily for 10 days**, within 48 h of contact.
Healthy low-risk adults do not need antivirals.

blocks.title: Antiretroviral classes (HIV)
rows: Chain terminators of reverse transcription; the backbone of most regimens
**Ritonavir** (or cobicistat) is used in low dose as a **booster**
Stop HIV DNA being inserted into the host genome
Enfuvirtide is the only ARV given by subcutaneous injection

blocks.title: Other antiviral facts
items: Start ART in **all** people with HIV regardless of CD4 count: **two NRTIs plus** a boosted protease inhibitor, an NNRTI or an integrase inhibitor. Aim for viral load <50 copies/mL within 3–6 months.
Hepatitis B: **entecavir and tenofovir** have replaced lamivudine and adefovir because they are more potent and resistance is much rarer.
Aciclovir does not clear latent virus, so recurrences still happen.
Palivizumab, a monoclonal antibody, prevents RSV in high-risk infants.

blocks.text: Aciclovir resistance usually comes from **viral thymidine kinase (or polymerase) mutations**. Ganciclovir still needs phosphorylation, so it may also fail. **Foscarnet** does not need activation, so it works against TK-deficient HSV and VZV.

blocks.title: Antifungal classes
rows: **Yeasts: Candida and Cryptococcus**; enters CSF; half-life about 30 h
Some non-albicans Candida are intrinsically resistant; all triazoles can prolong QTc
Yeasts, dermatophytes, dimorphic fungi, Aspergillus; reaches nails
Erratic absorption, so needs TDM; poor CSF levels
Needs TDM; photosensitivity, hepatitis, visual disturbance
Broad, including most **mucoraceous moulds**; posaconazole prophylaxis in high-risk haematology patients
Inhibit **beta-1,3-glucan** synthesis in the cell wall
IV only. **Candidaemia/systemic candidiasis**; caspofungin also for aspergillosis
**No activity against Cryptococcus or Mucorales**; few side effects
Broadest spectrum, **including Mucorales**; cryptococcal meningitis; empirical in neutropenic fever
Infusion reactions, **nephrotoxicity** (saline loading helps); lipid/liposomal forms much less toxic
Topical only: oral and vaginal candidiasis
Terbinafine is an allylamine concentrated in skin and sebum
Dermatophytes; **oral terbinafine for onychomycosis**; griseofulvin still used in children

blocks.title: Choosing an antifungal by infection
rows: Topical nystatin or clotrimazole; oral fluconazole
**Echinocandin** (micafungin first line) and **remove the central line**; Candida in blood culture is never a contaminant
**Surgical debridement + amphotericin B**, later step down to posaconazole or isavuconazole
**Amphotericin B ± flucytosine for 2 weeks** (induction), then fluconazole; repeated LPs for raised pressure
Neutropenic fever still present after ≥4 days of antibiotics
Add an antifungal: echinocandin, liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole or posaconazole

blocks.text: Know the gaps: **echinocandins miss Cryptococcus and Mucorales**; **fluconazole misses Aspergillus and Mucorales** and some non-albicans Candida; **voriconazole misses Mucorales**. For mucormycosis, think amphotericin (or posaconazole/isavuconazole).
Azoles **inhibit** cytochrome P450 and so **raise** levels of other drugs. Rifampicin **induces** P450 and **lowers** them. Expect exam questions that pair the two.

blocks.title: What drives resistance
items: Antibiotics for **viral infections** and other inappropriate uses.
**Doses that are too low** and **courses that are too long**.
Use of antimicrobials as **growth promoters in farming**.
**Any** antimicrobial use selects for resistance; **broad-spectrum empirical drugs** select more strongly than narrow ones because they touch more bacteria.
Resistance patterns vary from place to place (e.g. E. coli resistant to trimethoprim in one area, to nitrofurantoin in another), so **follow local guidelines**.

blocks.text: Resistance is either **intrinsic** (a natural property of the organism, e.g. M. bovis and pyrazinamide) or **acquired**, by spontaneous mutation or by **horizontal gene transfer**. **Plasmids** often carry resistance to several antibiotics at once and pass easily between Enterobacteriaceae. ESBLs and carbapenemases such as **NDM-1** spread this way.

blocks.title: Four mechanisms of resistance
rows: Staphylococcal penicillinase; ESBL, AmpC and NDM-1 in Enterobacteriaceae; chloramphenicol acetyltransferase

MRSA (altered PBP); VRE (altered peptidoglycan precursor); rifampicin-resistant TB (RNA polymerase mutation); ciprofloxacin resistance (DNA gyrase mutation); linezolid resistance (23S rRNA methylation)
Carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas (loss of porins); aminoglycosides in anaerobes (uptake needs oxygen)
Tetracycline resistance; fluconazole resistance in Candida

blocks.note: Look at: a bacterial cell showing the four resistance routes (impermeability, efflux, target change, enzyme breakdown), each labelled with a named example.

blocks.title: Antimicrobial stewardship: “Start Smart – Then Focus”
items: **Start smart:** in life-threatening infection, give empirical (“blind”) therapy immediately, but **take cultures first** and follow local policy.
**Then focus:** move from empirical to **targeted, narrow-spectrum** therapy as the organism and its sensitivities become known.
**72-hour review**, with five possible decisions: **stop**, **switch IV to oral**, **change** the drug, **continue IV**, or **OPAT**.
Switch IV to oral once the patient is **apyrexial and improving**; stop when there is no longer clinical evidence of infection; use the **shortest effective course**.
Stewardship tools include treatment guidelines, formularies and infection-specialist ward rounds.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.note: Look at: the three-step “Start Smart – Then Focus” scheme. Knowledge of the organism rises from empirical to targeted to susceptibility-guided therapy, while the spectrum used narrows.

blocks.title: Prophylaxis without overuse
items: Surgical prophylaxis rarely needs more than **24 hours**; for most operations a **single dose at induction** is enough.
Endocarditis prophylaxis is **not recommended** for dental, respiratory, GI or GU procedures in the UK.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.text: Stewardship and infection prevention and control feed each other: **good stewardship cuts health care-associated infections**, and **good infection control cuts the need for antibiotics**.

sections.title: Harms of misuse: C. difficile and penicillin-allergy labels

blocks.text: **Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile** is the **most common diagnosed cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea**. Antibiotics upset the colonic flora, and a patient exposed to spores becomes colonised with a toxin-producing strain (**toxins A and B**). Illness ranges from diarrhoea to **pseudomembranous colitis**, toxic dilatation and perforation. About **80% of cases occur in people over 65**. It usually starts in the first week of antibiotics but can appear **up to 6 weeks after they stop**. **Ribotype 027** is hypervirulent and makes more toxin.

blocks.title: Biggest culprits
items: **Second- and third-generation cephalosporins**
**Co-amoxiclav**
**Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin: also linked to ribotype 027)
**Clindamycin**
Proton-pump inhibitors may add to the risk.

blocks.title: Diagnosis
items: Healthy people carry C. difficile (about 5% of adults, up to 20% of elderly care-home residents), so **a positive culture alone is not diagnostic**.
**Two-step testing:** screen stool with **GDH** (an enzyme the organism makes) or **PCR/NAAT**, then confirm with a **toxin ELISA**.
Sigmoidoscopy may show adherent yellow-white pseudomembranes.
In an ill patient, take **abdominal and erect chest X-rays** to exclude toxic dilatation or perforation; CT if in doubt.

blocks.note: Look at: the colonoscopic view of pseudomembranous colitis, with many raised, adherent yellow-white plaques on the mucosa.

blocks.title: Managing C. difficile infection
rows: **Stop the precipitating antibiotic**, **isolate** the patient, give IV fluids
**Oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily for 10 days** or **oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 7–10 days**

Markers: WCC >15 ×10⁹/L, rising creatinine, temperature >38.5 °C, severe colitis. Use **oral vancomycin** and consider surgery early. KC Essentials says some centres use fidaxomicin here, but Davidson’s notes it has not been assessed in severe CDI
**Fidaxomicin** (fewer relapses than vancomycin) or tapering vancomycin; **faecal microbiota transplant** for repeated relapses
IV immunoglobulin and/or glucocorticoids are sometimes used

blocks.text: **Sources differ on first-line CDI treatment.** Davidson’s accepts **oral metronidazole or oral vancomycin**; vancomycin works better against ribotype 027 but costs more and may promote vancomycin resistance. Kumar and KC Essentials keep metronidazole for **mild/moderate** disease and use vancomycin for **severe** disease. Follow Davidson’s, and let severity guide the choice.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.title: The penicillin-allergy label
items: About 10% of patients say they are allergic to penicillin, but **around 90% of them are not truly IgE-allergic**.
A wrong label keeps patients from first-choice penicillins, and the alternatives used instead can give **worse outcomes**.
Always ask **what actually happened**: diarrhoea or nausea is a side effect, not allergy.
A rash after amoxicillin in **infectious mononucleosis** is very common (about 90% of cases in Kumar) and does **not** mean lasting allergy.
Refer selected patients for formal allergy testing; **desensitisation** is possible when a penicillin is essential.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection
Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.text: **Cross-reactivity figures disagree.** Davidson’s: real cross-reactivity with **1st-generation** cephalosporins, less with 2nd/3rd, and **avoid all cephalosporins after IgE-mediated penicillin allergy**; carbapenems about **1%**; **aztreonam** is least likely to cross-react. KC Essentials still quotes 10% for cephalosporins, Step-Up <2%. Kumar allows cautious cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam use in **non-severe** allergy. For the exam, follow Davidson’s.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

blocks.title: Extra hazards in older people
items: More C. difficile and more hypersensitivity (more previous exposure).
Renal impairment despite a “normal” creatinine: more nephrotoxicity (aminoglycosides, 1st-generation cephalosporins).
Beta-lactam accumulation can cause myoclonus, seizures or coma.
Quinolones cause delirium and lower the seizure threshold; reduced hepatic metabolism raises isoniazid hepatotoxicity.

cards.front: How do beta-lactams and glycopeptides differ in the way they stop cell-wall synthesis?
cards.back: Beta-lactams competitively inhibit transpeptidases (PBPs). Glycopeptides bind the D-alanine ends of peptidoglycan precursors.

cards.front: What is the molecular basis of MRSA?
cards.back: _mecA_ encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low beta-lactam affinity, so flucloxacillin cannot block cross-linking.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

cards.front: Which MRSA/GRE drug is dangerous with SSRIs, and why?
cards.back: Linezolid: it has MAO-inhibitor activity, so serotonin syndrome can result.

cards.front: Which Gram-positive agent must not be used for community-acquired pneumonia?
cards.back: Daptomycin (also watch the creatine kinase).

cards.front: Which cephalosporins cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
cards.back: Ceftazidime (3rd), cefepime (4th) and ceftobiprole (5th).

cards.front: Which penicillin-allergic patients should not get aztreonam?
cards.back: Those allergic to ceftazidime, which shares its side chain.

cards.front: Which carbapenem is used in meningitis, and why?
cards.back: Meropenem. Imipenem and ertapenem can cause seizures.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

cards.front: How is once-daily gentamicin dosed and monitored?
cards.back: 7 mg/kg; a level 6–14 h after the dose is plotted on the Hartford nomogram to choose a 24-, 36- or 48-hourly interval.

cards.front: Why can trimethoprim raise potassium?
cards.back: It is structurally like amiloride (a potassium-sparing diuretic). The risk is highest with ACE inhibitors.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

cards.front: What must be checked before starting ethambutol?
cards.back: Visual acuity (Snellen) and colour vision (Ishihara), because of optic neuritis.

cards.front: Define MDR-TB and XDR-TB.
cards.back: MDR: resistant to isoniazid + rifampicin. XDR: MDR plus any fluoroquinolone and at least one injectable (amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin).

cards.front: When should TB drugs be stopped for hepatitis?
cards.back: Only if bilirubin rises or transaminases exceed 3× normal; then reintroduce one at a time.

cards.front: Why does foscarnet work against aciclovir-resistant HSV?
cards.back: It is a pyrophosphate analogue that needs no viral thymidine kinase phosphorylation.

cards.front: What is the main toxicity of ganciclovir/valganciclovir?
cards.back: Myelosuppression, especially neutropenia.

cards.front: Which fungi do echinocandins not cover?
cards.back: Cryptococcus and the mucoraceous moulds.

cards.front: What is the induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis?
cards.back: Amphotericin B with flucytosine (about 2 weeks), then fluconazole. Flucytosine is never used alone.

cards.front: Name the four mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance.
cards.back: Enzymatic degradation, target modification, reduced permeability, active efflux.

cards.front: What are the five options at the 72-hour antibiotic review?
cards.back: Stop, switch IV to oral, change, continue IV, or OPAT.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

cards.front: Why is a toxin test needed to diagnose C. difficile infection?
cards.back: Asymptomatic carriage is common, so only toxin A/B detection (after a GDH or PCR screen) confirms disease.

cards.front: Which antibiotics carry the highest C. difficile risk?
cards.back: 2nd/3rd-generation cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, fluoroquinolones and clindamycin.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs has fever and a new murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus that is sensitive to meticillin. He has no drug allergies.
items.explanation: Meticillin-sensitive Staph. aureus: a **penicillinase-resistant penicillin (flucloxacillin)** is the mainstay. Benzylpenicillin fails because most staphylococci make penicillinase.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman on haemodialysis has rigors during dialysis. Blood cultures from her tunnelled line grow meticillin-resistant Staph. aureus. She needs an intravenous agent, and drug levels can be monitored on the unit.
items.explanation: MRSA bacteraemia: **IV vancomycin**, with pre-dose levels kept above 10 mg/L (15–20 mg/L in serious staphylococcal infection). Flucloxacillin is useless against MRSA because of PBP2a.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a central-line bacteraemia with Enterococcus faecium resistant to vancomycin and teicoplanin. He takes high-dose sertraline for severe depression that his psychiatrist does not want stopped. An IV bactericidal agent is chosen.
items.explanation: Two steps: (1) glycopeptide-resistant enterococci are treated with linezolid, tigecycline or daptomycin; (2) linezolid has MAO-inhibitor activity and with an SSRI risks serotonin syndrome. So **daptomycin**, a bactericidal IV lipopeptide, is chosen.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with pyelonephritis grows an ESBL-producing E. coli. She is now stable and is to finish 10 more days of IV therapy at home through the outpatient (OPAT) service, which needs a once-daily drug.
items.explanation: Serious ESBL infection needs a carbapenem, and **ertapenem** is given once daily, so it suits OPAT. Its lack of Pseudomonas cover does not matter here.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin last year. He now has a Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. He has never had ceftazidime. A beta-lactam is wanted.
items.explanation: **Aztreonam** is the beta-lactam least likely to cross-react in penicillin allergy and covers aerobic Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas. Cephalosporins are avoided after IgE-mediated penicillin allergy.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops meningitis after neurosurgery. The CSF grows an ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. A carbapenem is needed, and she has had a seizure before.
items.explanation: Two steps: ESBL means a carbapenem; in CNS infection, imipenem and ertapenem lower the seizure threshold, so **meropenem** is the carbapenem used for meningitis.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man in ICU has ventilator pneumonia caused by a carbapenemase-producing Acinetobacter baumannii, resistant to all beta-lactams and to ciprofloxacin and gentamicin.
items.explanation: **Colistin** disrupts the Gram-negative outer membrane and remains active against Acinetobacter and carbapenemase producers. It is a last-resort drug: watch kidneys and nerves.

Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man started standard quadruple therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis 7 weeks ago. He now says his vision is blurred and he can no longer tell red from green on traffic lights.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: **Ethambutol** causes optic (retrobulbar) neuritis with red–green colour loss and reduced acuity. Acuity and colour vision should be checked before starting; stopping the drug usually lets vision recover.
whyNot: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, not optic neuritis with colour loss.
Rifampicin colours tears orange but does not damage the optic nerve.
Pyrazinamide causes hepatitis, raised urate and arthralgia.
Pyridoxine is given to prevent isoniazid neuropathy; it does not cause visual loss.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is in the second month of treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis. He wakes with a hot, swollen and exquisitely tender first metatarsophalangeal joint. Serum urate is raised.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: **Pyrazinamide** raises serum uric acid and can trigger acute gout. It is given only in the 2-month initial phase.
whyNot: Isoniazid causes hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy, not hyperuricaemia.
Rifampicin causes orange secretions, enzyme induction and hepatitis.
Ethambutol mainly causes optic neuritis.
Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy and does not affect urate.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, headache, odd behaviour and a seizure. CSF PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus.
items.explanation: HSV encephalitis is treated with **IV aciclovir** for 2–3 weeks. Oral prodrugs are not used for encephalitis.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 25 cells/mm³) has painful genital herpes ulcers that have kept growing despite high-dose aciclovir. The lab finds a viral thymidine kinase mutation.
items.explanation: Two steps: TK mutation means aciclovir (and ganciclovir) cannot be activated; **foscarnet** needs no phosphorylation, so it works against TK-deficient HSV.

items.stem: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient has rising CMV viraemia with fever and leucopenia. He is well enough to go home and can swallow tablets.
items.explanation: CMV is treated with ganciclovir; the **oral prodrug valganciclovir** suits an outpatient. Watch for neutropenia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old aid worker becomes febrile and unwell after returning from rural Sierra Leone. Lassa fever is confirmed by the reference laboratory.
items.explanation: **IV ribavirin** is the antiviral for Lassa fever. Its most frequent adverse effect is haemolytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is in week 2 of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia for acute myeloid leukaemia. He develops fever, cough and haemoptysis. CT chest shows new nodules, and bronchoalveolar lavage grows Aspergillus fumigatus.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is the preferred treatment?
questions.explanation: This is invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. **Voriconazole** is the main drug for aspergillosis (needs drug-level monitoring; watch for visual disturbance, photosensitivity and hepatitis).
whyNot: Fluconazole covers yeasts (Candida, Cryptococcus) but not Aspergillus.
Nystatin is too toxic for systemic use and is only topical.
Terbinafine is for dermatophyte skin and nail infection.
Griseofulvin is a dermatophyte drug used mainly in children.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 40 cells/mm³) has 2 weeks of headache and fever. CSF opening pressure is raised and India ink stain shows encapsulated yeasts.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate initial antifungal treatment?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis needs induction with **amphotericin B plus flucytosine** (about 2 weeks), then fluconazole, with repeated LPs for raised pressure.
whyNot: Fluconazole is used for consolidation after induction, not alone as first treatment of severe meningitis.
Echinocandins have no activity against Cryptococcus.
Flucytosine alone leads quickly to resistance and must always be combined.
Nystatin is topical only.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man was started on IV co-amoxiclav for community-acquired pneumonia. At 72 hours he has been apyrexial for 36 hours, is eating, and his CRP is falling. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae fully sensitive to penicillin.
questions.leadIn: What is the best antibiotic decision now?
questions.explanation: “Start Smart – Then Focus”: at the 72-hour review he is improving and the organism is known, so **switch IV to oral and narrow the spectrum** (oral amoxicillin).
whyNot: Staying on broad IV therapy adds line risks and selection pressure with no benefit.
Escalating to a carbapenem is the opposite of stewardship and is not needed.
There is no MRSA, so vancomycin adds toxicity only.
Ciprofloxacin is weak against pneumococci and strongly linked to C. difficile.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

questions.stem: A Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate from a ventilated patient is resistant to meropenem. Molecular testing finds no carbapenemase gene, but expression of an outer-membrane porin is markedly reduced.
questions.leadIn: Which resistance mechanism is this?
options: Reduced permeability of the cell envelope
questions.explanation: Carbapenem resistance in Pseudomonas is the textbook example of **reduced permeability** (loss of porins); increased efflux may add to it.
whyNot: There is no carbapenemase, so the drug is not being destroyed.
Altered PBP is the MRSA mechanism.
D-Ala-D-Lac precursors explain VRE.
Gyrase mutations cause quinolone resistance.

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.
questions.theme: Next step in suspected C. difficile infection

items.stem: An 81-year-old care-home resident has had watery diarrhoea 5 times a day since finishing cefuroxime a week ago. The stool glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) screen is positive.
items.explanation: GDH only shows the organism is present, and carriage is common in the elderly. A positive screen must be confirmed by a **toxin assay**.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has toxin-positive C. difficile infection. Temperature 38.9 °C, WCC 23 ×10⁹/L and creatinine rising from his baseline. The abdomen is soft and not distended.
items.explanation: Fever >38.5 °C, WCC >15 and rising creatinine mark **severe** disease, so give **oral vancomycin**. Davidson’s notes that fidaxomicin has not been assessed in severe CDI.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has her third episode of C. difficile infection in 6 months, despite courses of vancomycin and then fidaxomicin.
items.explanation: Repeated relapses after vancomycin and fidaxomicin: **faecal microbiota transplant** restores a healthy colonic flora.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man with toxin-positive C. difficile infection becomes unwell. His stool frequency has fallen, but his abdomen is distended and tender and his pulse is 120/min.
items.explanation: Two steps: fewer stools with a distended abdomen in CDI suggests ileus or toxic dilatation, not recovery. Take **abdominal and erect chest X-rays** to look for dilatation or perforation.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man on long-term prednisolone for polymyalgia is treated for a urinary infection. On day 4 he feels a sudden snap at the back of his ankle while climbing stairs.
items.explanation: Achilles tendon rupture is a classic **fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin)** effect, with older age and corticosteroids raising the risk.

items.stem: During a 20-minute infusion for MRSA bacteraemia, a 45-year-old woman develops flushing and itching over her face, neck and upper chest. Blood pressure is stable.
items.explanation: Too-rapid **vancomycin** infusion releases histamine: the “red man” reaction. Slow the infusion.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man being treated for a Bacteroides liver abscess vomits violently and flushes after drinking beer at a party.
items.explanation: **Metronidazole** causes a disulfiram-like (Antabuse) reaction with alcohol.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man on ramipril for heart failure is treated for a lower urinary tract infection. Five days later his potassium is 6.3 mmol/L.
items.explanation: **Trimethoprim** is structurally like amiloride and blocks potassium excretion; the ACE inhibitor adds to it.

Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man is receiving IV daptomycin for MRSA tricuspid endocarditis. After 2 weeks he reports aching, weak thigh muscles.
questions.leadIn: Which blood test is most useful?
questions.explanation: Daptomycin can raise **creatine kinase**, so CK is the test to check in a patient with muscle symptoms.
whyNot: Amylase is for pancreatitis, not a daptomycin effect.
Hypothyroidism can cause myopathy but is not the drug-related cause here.
Raised urate is a pyrazinamide effect.
B12 is relevant to neuropathy, not this drug-related myalgia.

questions.stem: A foundation doctor asks why gentamicin is now given as a single large daily dose rather than small doses three times a day.
questions.leadIn: Which is the best explanation?
options: Its killing depends on the time the level stays above the MIC
Its killing rises with the peak level relative to the MIC
A single dose achieves useful CSF levels
It loses activity when bacterial numbers are high
Divided doses cause less drug accumulation
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides show **concentration-dependent killing**: efficacy increases with Cmax : MIC. A high once-daily dose also lets levels fall between doses, which lowers toxicity.
whyNot: Time above MIC drives beta-lactams and vancomycin, not aminoglycosides.
Aminoglycoside CSF penetration is negligible whatever the regimen.
Aminoglycosides are not subject to an inoculum effect; beta-lactams are.
High once-daily dosing reduces accumulation and toxicity, not divided dosing.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant needs an antibiotic.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is contraindicated at this stage of pregnancy?
questions.explanation: **Trimethoprim** is a folate antagonist and is teratogenic in the first trimester. Penicillins, cephalosporins, erythromycin and clindamycin are not known to be harmful.
whyNot: Penicillins are not known to be harmful in pregnancy.
Cephalosporins are not known to be harmful.
Erythromycin is listed as not known to be harmful.
Clindamycin is listed as not known to be harmful.

questions.stem: A sputum isolate of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is reported as “MDR”.
questions.leadIn: Which resistance pattern does this term mean?
options: Isoniazid, rifampicin, a fluoroquinolone and an injectable agent
questions.explanation: **MDR-TB = resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin.** Add a fluoroquinolone and at least one injectable and it becomes XDR-TB.
whyNot: Rifampicin mono-resistance is not MDR by definition.
That pattern defines XDR-TB.
MDR does not need resistance to pyrazinamide or ethambutol.
Isoniazid mono-resistance is not MDR.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man develops high fever, confusion and a dry cough a few days after staying at a hotel where a cooling-tower outbreak has been reported. His urinary Legionella antigen test is positive. He wants a short oral course.
items.explanation: Step 1: a hotel cooling-tower outbreak and a positive urinary Legionella antigen identify **Legionella pneumophila**. Step 2: Legionella is treated with a macrolide (**azithromycin**), levofloxacin or doxycycline, not with beta-lactams; azithromycin is the only one of these offered here.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has spreading, well-demarcated erythema of the leg. Swab of a skin break grows group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (Strep. pyogenes). She is not allergic to anything.
items.explanation: Step 1: identify the organism, Strep. pyogenes. Step 2: it has stayed **penicillin-sensitive worldwide**, so plain **benzylpenicillin** is the narrowest effective choice; there is no need for broader cover.

items.stem: A 64-year-old ventilated man has a hospital-acquired pneumonia. Sputum grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa sensitive to piperacillin–tazobactam and meropenem; there is no ESBL. A single beta-lactam is wanted.
items.explanation: Step 1: the organism is Pseudomonas, which rules out amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav and ceftriaxone, and a beta-lactam is wanted, which rules out gentamicin and colistin. Step 2: of the two active beta-lactams, choose the narrower one and keep the carbapenem in reserve: **piperacillin–tazobactam**. Meropenem would work, but there is no ESBL to justify it.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman admitted with cellulitis has “penicillin allergy” on her chart. Asked what happened, she says she had a widespread itchy rash at age 16 when she was given amoxicillin for a sore throat that turned out to be glandular fever. She has had no reaction since.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of her label?
options: A true IgE-mediated allergy; avoid all beta-lactams for life
An aminopenicillin rash linked to infectious mononucleosis, not proof of lasting allergy
A cephalosporin will cross-react in about half of such patients
Only aztreonam may be used for her cellulitis
She must be desensitised before any penicillin is given
questions.explanation: Reason it through: (1) Ask what the reaction was and when. (2) A rash with amoxicillin during **infectious mononucleosis** is extremely common and **does not mean lasting allergy**. (3) Most reported penicillin allergies (around 90%) are not IgE-mediated, and a wrong label drives broader, worse treatment. She should be referred for formal allergy assessment and the label reviewed.
whyNot: There was no anaphylaxis, urticaria with angioedema or wheeze, and the context explains the rash.
Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins is far lower than this, even in true allergy.
Aztreonam is for proven severe allergy and has no Gram-positive cover, so it would fail in streptococcal cellulitis.
Desensitisation is for confirmed allergy when a penicillin is essential, not for a doubtful label.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has had thickened, yellow, crumbling toenails for 2 years. Nail clippings grow Trichophyton rubrum.
items.explanation: Dermatophyte onychomycosis: **oral terbinafine**, which concentrates in skin, sebum and nail. Rarely it causes liver toxicity.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman in ICU after bowel surgery has fever and needs vasopressors. Blood cultures from her central line grow Candida glabrata. She is not neutropenic.
items.explanation: Candidaemia in an unstable, non-neutropenic patient: an **echinocandin** (e.g. caspofungin) plus removal of the central line. Fluconazole is considered only in stable patients without prior azole exposure, and some non-albicans species are intrinsically resistant to it.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman recovering from diabetic ketoacidosis develops facial pain and swelling with necrotic ulceration inside the nose. Sinus biopsy grows Rhizopus. She has had surgical debridement.
items.explanation: Two steps: Rhizopus after DKA means **mucormycosis**; Mucorales are missed by voriconazole and echinocandins, so first-line is debridement plus **amphotericin B**.

items.stem: A 73-year-old man who uses a steroid inhaler for COPD has white plaques on his tongue that scrape off, leaving a red base. He takes several drugs metabolised by cytochrome P450, and the pharmacist asks for a treatment that will not raise their levels.
items.explanation: Two steps: (1) oral thrush can be treated topically or with an oral azole; (2) azoles inhibit cytochrome P450 and raise levels of other drugs, so choose topical **nystatin** suspension, which is not absorbed from the mouth (it is too toxic for systemic use).

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.
options: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months
The same four-drug start, with total treatment extended to 12 months
Isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol, without pyrazinamide
A second-line regimen built on a fluoroquinolone, an injectable agent and linezolid

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 30 cells/mm³) has fever, night sweats, weight loss and anaemia. Blood cultures grow Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare.
items.explanation: Disseminated **M. avium-intracellulare** in advanced HIV resists standard TB therapy and is treated with **ethambutol, rifabutin and clarithromycin**.

items.stem: A 48-year-old dairy farmer who drinks unpasteurised milk has a chronically enlarged cervical lymph node. Culture grows Mycobacterium bovis.
items.explanation: Two steps: the organism is **M. bovis**, which is intrinsically resistant to pyrazinamide, so the regimen is **isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol**.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has 3 weeks of headache, fever and drowsiness. CSF culture grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis fully sensitive to first-line drugs.
items.explanation: Tuberculous meningitis is treated with the standard four-drug start but for **12 months in total**, not 6.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with pulmonary TB has sputum showing resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin, with fluoroquinolones still active.
items.explanation: Resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin is **MDR-TB**, which needs a specialist **second-line regimen** (e.g. a fluoroquinolone, an injectable such as amikacin, and linezolid).

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with COPD develops fever, myalgia and cough during a local influenza outbreak. Symptoms started 30 hours ago. He is not hypoxic.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate antiviral management?
options: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days
Oral oseltamivir 75 mg once daily for 10 days
No antiviral, as he presented after 24 hours
questions.explanation: He is high-risk (chronic lung disease) and within 48 hours of onset, so he should get **treatment-dose oseltamivir, 75 mg twice daily for 5 days**. The neuraminidase inhibitor stops new virus being released from infected cells.
whyNot: Amantadine is no longer recommended because resistance is widespread and it covers influenza A only.
Aciclovir is for herpesviruses and has no anti-influenza activity.
Once daily for 10 days is the post-exposure prophylaxis regimen, not treatment.
The treatment window is 48 hours, not 24.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman on citalopram has been taking oral linezolid for 5 days for an MRSA wound infection. She becomes agitated and sweaty, with tremor, inducible clonus and a temperature of 38.6 °C.
questions.leadIn: Which property of linezolid explains this?
questions.explanation: Linezolid has **MAO-inhibitor activity**; with an SSRI it can cause **serotonin syndrome** (agitation, clonus, hyperthermia).
whyNot: Linezolid does not induce P450; rifampicin is the classic inducer.
QT prolongation is a macrolide or fluoroquinolone problem and would not cause clonus.
Histamine release is the vancomycin “red man” reaction.
Linezolid has no dopamine-blocking action.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with bronchiectasis grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Two years ago he had anaphylaxis during an infusion of ceftazidime. He has never reacted to penicillins.
questions.leadIn: Which antipseudomonal agent should be avoided?
questions.explanation: **Aztreonam** shares a side chain with **ceftazidime**, so a ceftazidime-allergic patient may react to it. This is the one important exception to aztreonam’s safety in beta-lactam allergy.
whyNot: Ciprofloxacin is not a beta-lactam and covers Pseudomonas.
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside with no beta-lactam cross-reactivity.
Colistin is a polymyxin, unrelated to ceftazidime.
Amikacin is an aminoglycoside, unrelated to ceftazidime.

questions.stem: A ward audit finds that many elderly patients with no diarrhoea have C. difficile isolated from stool culture.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason the diagnosis of C. difficile infection relies on toxin detection?
options: Culture takes too long to be useful
Asymptomatic carriage is common, especially in care-home residents
Toxin assays are cheaper than culture
Only hypervirulent strains grow in culture
questions.explanation: C. difficile is found in about 5% of healthy adults and up to 20% of elderly people in residential care, so finding the organism does not prove disease. **Toxin A/B detection** (after a GDH or PCR screen) confirms infection.
whyNot: Speed is not the main issue; even a positive culture can be a carrier.
Cost is not the reason for the toxin-based approach.
Ordinary and hypervirulent strains both grow.
Spores can germinate and grow; this is not the reason.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the most suitable option from the list. An option may fit several patients, one patient or none.

items.stem: A Staphylococcus aureus blood isolate is resistant to flucloxacillin and to co-amoxiclav. PCR detects the mecA gene.
items.explanation: _mecA_ codes for **PBP2a**, which has low affinity for beta-lactams. A beta-lactamase inhibitor cannot help, because the target, not the drug, has changed.

items.stem: An Enterococcus faecium isolate from a urinary catheter is resistant to both vancomycin and teicoplanin.
items.explanation: In VRE the precursor ends in **D-Ala-D-Lac**, so glycopeptides cannot bind.

items.stem: A patient previously treated for TB relapses. A rapid molecular test on sputum shows resistance to rifampicin.
items.explanation: Rifampicin resistance comes from mutations in the **beta-subunit of RNA polymerase**, and usually goes with isoniazid resistance (MDR-TB).

cites.chapter: Sepsis and the treatment of bacterial infection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old kidney transplant recipient has been on oral prophylaxis against cytomegalovirus for 6 weeks. Routine bloods show neutrophils 0.6 ×10⁹/L, down from 4.2 before the course. Haemoglobin is stable.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: **Valganciclovir** (the oral ganciclovir prodrug) is used against CMV, and **neutropenia** is its main toxicity.
whyNot: Aciclovir has very little marrow toxicity.
Oseltamivir mainly causes GI upset.
Ribavirin causes haemolytic anaemia, and the haemoglobin is stable.
Foscarnet is IV and causes renal and electrolyte problems rather than isolated neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman develops a severe community-acquired pneumonia a week after influenza. Sputum and blood cultures grow meticillin-resistant Staph. aureus.
questions.leadIn: Which agent should be avoided for this infection?
questions.explanation: **Daptomycin is not effective for community-acquired pneumonia**, even though it kills MRSA and is used for MRSA bacteraemia, endocarditis and skin infection.
whyNot: Vancomycin is a standard MRSA treatment.
Linezolid is an oral or IV option for MRSA.
Teicoplanin is a glycopeptide active against MRSA.
Ceftaroline is a 5th-generation cephalosporin with MRSA activity.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is 3 weeks into isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He feels well. ALT is twice the upper limit of normal and bilirubin is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Continue treatment and monitor liver function
Halve the dose of every drug
questions.explanation: A mild transaminase rise is common. Drugs are stopped only if **bilirubin rises or transaminases exceed three times normal**; then they are restarted one at a time. Here, **continue and monitor**.
whyNot: Stopping now interrupts curative treatment without meeting the stopping threshold.
There is no indication yet to drop pyrazinamide.
Swapping out the key sterilising drug weakens the regimen without reason.
Under-dosing promotes resistance and failure.

ospe.identify: Pseudomembranous colitis: many raised, adherent yellow-white plaques on inflamed colonic mucosa. This is C. difficile infection after antibiotics.
Hartford nomogram: read the gentamicin/tobramycin level at its hour after a 7 mg/kg dose to choose a 24-, 36- or 48-hourly dosing interval.
Pharmacodynamic curve: identify Cmax, the MIC line, time above MIC and AUC. Aminoglycosides depend on Cmax : MIC; beta-lactams and vancomycin depend on time above MIC.
Resistance mechanisms diagram: impermeability (carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas), efflux (tetracyclines), target change (MRSA, VRE) and enzyme breakdown (ESBL, NDM-1).
